title: LifePilot: Building a Personal Life Manager Inside a Chat Room
author: Sushil Ghimire
summary: Flip the Switch Hackathon 2026 A build log on three agents, one human veto, and what happened when our agent quota ran out. Introduction Most agent demos follow the same script. You type something, the agent does it, and everyone in the room is impressed for about ten seconds. We wanted to build the opposite. We wanted an agent that stops and asks before it changes anything in your life. That idea became LifePilot, a personal life organizer that runs inside a chat room. It has three agents that share one room with one human. The rule they all follow is simple: propose first, save later. This post explains what we built, how Switch fits into it, and the moment our build hit a wall we did not plan for. It is written for someone who has never used Switch before and wants to know what it feels like to build on it. The problem we started with Most people keep their life in too many places. A notes app for ideas. Two group chats for plans. A photo of a handwritten list. The rest stays in memory, which is the least reliable place of all. The bill that was due last Tuesday was never written down anywhere. Nobody forgot on purpose. It just never had a home. Most productivity tools solve this by taking over. They ask for an account, sync everything to a server, and quietly decide what matters on your behalf. For something as personal as your day, that trade is wrong. LifePilot takes the other position. It keeps your data on your own machine, it shows you exactly what it understood, and it refuses to change a single record until you say yes. Why we built it as a chat room We could have built a web app. We chose not to, for three reasons. The room already exists. If you have Telegram or Discord on your phone, you already have LifePilot. There is no app to install on the user's side, no login screen, and no URL to remember. The room remembers. Tomorrow's morning briefing lands in the same place where you set today's task. Your context never resets because a page reloaded. Saying yes is visible. Approval happens in plain text, in front of you. It is not hidden inside a settings menu or a pop up you click without reading. The last point became the center of the whole design. How Switch fits in Switch is an open source tool that connects an AI agent you already use to a team chat app such as Slack, Teams, Discord or Telegram. You install Switch Console, create a room, and connect agents to it. For us, Switch is not a small part of this project. It is the reason the project makes sense. One room holds the whole product. #lifepilot contains the human and the three agents. There is no separate admin panel, dashboard or backend UI. Three agents, three jobs. Capture, Planner and Reminder each have their own instructions. One general purpose chatbot trying to do all three would be a worse product and a worse demo. The conversation is the history. You can scroll up and see what was proposed, what you rejected, and what you approved. The approval is public. Other people in the room can see that the agent asked before it acted. That changes how much you trust it. Take Switch out of LifePilot and what remains is a task parser with an API. Nothing you would want to open every morning. The three agents LifePilot runs three agents with narrow responsibilities. Agent What it does What it never does Capture Turns a sentence into a structured task or bill Does not save anything until you approve Planner Builds a short daily plan Does not create tasks on its own Reminder Warns about tasks due today and bills coming up Does not repeat itself or nag The daily plan has a hard limit of three items. It is ranked by deadline first, then priority, then estimated effort. A list of twelve things is not a plan, it is a wish. The design rule that shaped everything Every Switch agent in LifePilot is a thin shell. That means the agent itself does very little thinking. It does not guess dates. It does not rank priorities. It does not invent categories. It sends one command to the backend and posts the reply it gets back. curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8000/chat \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"message": "finish biology notes by Friday", "sender": "capture-room"}' The backend sends back JSON. The reply field already contains the understanding and the question, and the agent posts it to the room word for word: Capture: I understood "Finish biology notes" as study, priority 3, due 2026-11-13, about 45 min. Nothing is saved yet. Reply "yes" to save it or "no" to discard. If you say no, nothing is written. Not marked as deleted, not saved with a flag. Nothing enters the database at all. This leads to the one sentence that describes the whole project: The model decides what the words mean. The code decides what is allowed to be stored. Those are two separate jobs, and we kept them in two separate places. Why the approval rule has two layers We enforce the "ask first" rule twice, on purpose. Layer one is the instruction. Each agent is told, in its Switch instructions, to show what it understood and wait for a yes. Layer two is the database. The backend will not write a task unless the request carries an approved flag. If the flag is missing, the write does not happen, no matter how convincing the message was. A prompt is not a guarantee. An agent can be confused, and an instruction can be talked around. A database constraint cannot be argued with. If you only trust the prompt, your safety disappears the moment the model behaves unexpectedly. If you only trust the code, the user never sees the question. We wanted both the visible question and the enforced answer. This is also the part of LifePilot that is easiest to test. There is a test that sends a proposal, never sends a yes, and then checks that the task table is still empty. That test does not care which model is running. What actually happened during the build Getting the room running We installed Switch Console and used Switch Buddy, the admin agent that comes with Console, to get the workspace and the room set up. Switch Buddy is part of Switch itself, not something we made. Then we created two agents of our own and connected both to the room: Agenty and Agentex . It worked. Watching an agent answer inside a real chat channel for the first time is a genuinely good moment, and it took far less time than we expected. Then the quota ran out Before we finished the project, our AI agent subscriptions hit their usage limit . The agents stopped replying. It was not Switch that ran out. Switch is free and open source and you run it yourself. What ran out was the subscription behind each agent, the Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode account that gives the agent its ability to reason. Those plans are metered by session, by time window, or by week. When the allowance is gone, the agent has nothing to think with. Every team building with agents pays this cost. Few plan for it. What still worked when the agents stopped Because every agent was a thin shell, most of LifePilot was not affected by the agents going quiet. python -m backend.main --demo That one command runs the whole product. Capture reads messages. Planner builds the day. Reminder produces warnings. A full working day of behavior prints to the terminal with no agent, no network connection, and no quota. The test suite still passed. The rules still ran. The database still behaved. If we had put the reasoning inside the agent instructions instead, by writing date parsing into a prompt or asking the model to rank tasks in natural language, the quota running out would have deleted the project. We would have had nothing to run and nothing to show. All our work would have been a set of prompts we could no longer execute. Put your logic where quota cannot reach it. An agent is a delivery channel. It should not be the place where your product lives. What we would do differently Three changes we would make: Budget the agent usage before building, not after. Decide which agent does what, and estimate how many sessions that takes. We connected our agents and spent the allowance while we were still finding out what they could do. Build the offline demo on the first day. Ours is a single flag, --demo , and it saved us. Write yours before you need it, because demos get recorded at the end of a hackathon, when your quota is at its lowest. Keep the agent as a shell. Every extra piece of reasoning you move into the prompt costs money, is harder to test, and makes the product depend on a service that can stop answering. A short checklist if you are starting now Check your plan limits first. Find out what one agent session costs you before you connect anything. Get one agent answering in a channel before you design anything else. Switch's quickstart is short, and seeing it work changes how you plan the rest. Decide what the agent may do without asking. For LifePilot the answer was "nothing". Decide yours before you connect it, not after. Write the demonstration you can run offline. Even a simple one. It is insurance against the worst possible timing. Keep the agent instructions short. Thin instructions plus a real backend are easier to debug than a long prompt that tries to be the backend. What we would build next The backend is finished. The room template defines all three agents with their instructions, their addressing rules and their approval behavior. The test suite passes and the demo runs without a network connection. The next step is the one we did not get to before the quota ran out. That step is bringing LifePilot's own three agents, not placeholder ones, into a live Switch room, and watching a real person say no to a real proposal and see that nothing was saved. Everything we built points at that moment. It is the reason the two layer approval exists. Running it yourself If you want to see the parts that work without an agent: python -m venv .venv .venv \S cripts \a ctivate pip install -r requirements.txt python -m backend.main --demo python -m backend.main --check --demo runs a full day of behavior in the terminal and needs no network connection. --check reports your setup, hides your API key so it is never printed, and can send one live test request to the model you chose. The backend works with any provider that offers an OpenAI compatible endpoint, including free ones. If no key is configured it falls back to deterministic rules, so it never stops working. The test suite covers 105 cases and runs without any network access. Closing LifePilot started as an argument about trust. We did not want an assistant that quietly rearranges your life. We wanted one that shows you its understanding, waits for a yes, and cannot save anything without one. Switch made that argument real, because the conversation is the interface. The approval happens where you can see it. We ran out of agent quota before we finished. In the end that turned out to be useful. It showed us that we had put the important parts in the right place. Built for the Flip the Switch hackathon by WeMakeDevs, DevTools Academy and Switch. Switch is open source and free to self host.

title: OpsMemory AI: Turning Everyday Business Incidents into Operational Intelligence
author: Indu R
summary: OpsMemory AI: Turning Everyday Business Incidents into Operational Intelligence Small businesses make dozens of operational decisions every day. When should a courier collect parcels? Which response actually resolves a recurring delivery problem? What should the team do differently the next time an incident occurs? These decisions often depend on experience. Yet that experience is rarely captured in a way that can be retrieved and reused. A problem gets solved, the team moves on, and the details gradually disappear into conversations, messages, and individual memory. When the same issue returns, people may repeat the same ineffective response or start investigating from scratch. OpsMemory AI explores a different approach: an operations intelligence agent that uses remembered business experience to inform future decisions. Rather than treating every operational question as a new problem, it connects incidents, actions, and recorded outcomes through persistent memory. The problem: businesses forget what they learn Imagine a small business experiencing repeated courier delays. The team knows that deliveries have been late, but knowing that a problem happened is not the same as knowing what response worked. Consider two possible actions: Remind the courier team about the existing pickup schedule. Request an earlier pickup slot. Both actions sound reasonable. But which one has supporting evidence from the business's own experience? A conventional chatbot might provide general suggestions. An operations memory agent should instead look for relevant past incidents and outcomes before recommending a next step. That distinction is the foundation of OpsMemory AI. The idea: operational memory as a decision-making resource OpsMemory AI is a lightweight application designed to help small businesses preserve operational knowledge and make it useful again. Its central principle is simple: An incident should not end when it is resolved. The experience should remain available to inform the next decision. The system brings together three important pieces of information: Incident: What happened? Action: What did the team do? Outcome: What happened after that action? These records provide context for future operational decisions. The project uses Hindsight as its persistent memory layer. Instead of relying only on the current conversation, the application can retain operational information and retrieve relevant memories later. How the system works The current prototype follows a straightforward workflow. 1. Capture an operational incident The application records an incident in a structured format. For example: Three customer deliveries were delayed because the courier failed to collect parcels on time. This creates a record of the operational problem rather than leaving it only in someone's memory. 2. Record the action and its outcome The team records what it tried and what happened afterward. In the demonstration scenario, the business requested an earlier courier pickup slot. The next day's deliveries arrived on time. This feedback matters because an action without an outcome is incomplete operational knowledge. 3. Retain and retrieve memories using Hindsight Hindsight provides the persistent memory layer. The application sends operational information to Hindsight and retrieves relevant memories when generating an evidence-based recommendation. This makes the memory system part of the application's actual workflow, rather than an optional feature or a decorative chatbot history. The prototype also exposes retrieved memories in its interface so that users can inspect the information behind a recommendation. 4. Compare recorded experience OpsMemory AI presents recorded actions and their outcomes so that users can distinguish between an action with a positive recorded result and one that did not resolve the problem. In the current demonstration, the successful earlier-pickup example is available in Hindsight-backed memory. A separate unsuccessful reminder example is stored in the application's local feedback data and displayed for comparison. This distinction is intentional: the interface should make the source of evidence clear rather than imply that every displayed record came from the same memory source. 5. Produce a cautious recommendation Based on the available evidence, the prototype identifies the earlier pickup request as the best-supported recorded action. It also communicates an important limitation: the recommendation is based on one distinct successful feedback record. It does not claim statistical certainty or prove that the action caused the improvement. For operational decision-making, showing the strength and limits of evidence is just as important as producing a recommendation. Technology behind the prototype The application combines a small set of technologies: Python: Core application logic and integration. Streamlit: Interactive user interface. Hindsight: Persistent memory retention and retrieval. Ollama with Llama 3.2 1B: Local language-model infrastructure. JSON: Structured storage for the prototype's operational records. The application is designed to run locally. This made it possible to experiment with persistent memory and language-model integration without depending on a paid hosted model API. The architecture is deliberately lightweight, making the prototype easier to inspect, run, and extend. A design decision: make memory visible One important design choice was to make retrieved memory visible to the user. AI recommendations can be difficult to trust when the application does not explain where they came from. OpsMemory AI therefore presents historical memory alongside its recommendation. A user can inspect the retrieved context and understand why a particular action is being highlighted. This also makes the prototype easier to evaluate. Rather than simply displaying a confident-sounding answer, it exposes the evidence available to the system. The goal is not to make the agent appear certain. The goal is to make its reasoning more inspectable. What I learned while building it Building a memory-driven application involves more than connecting an LLM to a database. One challenge was integrating a persistent memory service into an interactive application without making the user interface depend on fragile execution patterns. Another was handling the difference between structured application records and memories extracted by the memory system. A single operational event can be represented as several separate facts, so retrieval needs to be evaluated in context. A third challenge was avoiding exaggerated conclusions. A prototype with a small number of examples cannot establish that a recommendation will work across every business or situation. It can, however, demonstrate a useful architecture: capture experience, retain it, retrieve relevant context, and present evidence with appropriate limitations. These constraints shaped the current implementation. Current limitations and next steps OpsMemory AI is an early prototype, not a production-ready business operations platform. Its current demonstration uses a small courier-delivery dataset. The recommendation is based on limited recorded experience, and the application does not yet have enough data to measure long-term improvements in delivery performance. Future development could include: More operational categories, such as inventory, customer support, and scheduling. Larger incident and feedback datasets. Time-based analysis of recurring problems. Stronger evaluation of memory retrieval quality. User permissions and audit trails. Recommendation confidence based on the quantity and quality of supporting evidence. Integrations with the tools small businesses already use. The longer-term direction is an operational knowledge system that becomes more useful as a business accumulates experience. Final thoughts The most valuable information in a small business is not always found in a formal document. It is often hidden in the decisions people make, the problems they solve, and the outcomes they observe. OpsMemory AI is an experiment in preserving that knowledge and making it available when a similar decision appears again. The larger idea is straightforward: A business should not have to learn the same operational lesson twice simply because it forgot what happened the first time. By combining persistent memory with evidence-based recommendations, OpsMemory AI explores how AI agents can move beyond answering questions and begin helping organizations build on their own experience.

title: Why Your Base64 Won't Decode: A Practical Checklist for Validating Base64 Strings
author: Mind vs Drive
summary: You copy a Base64 string out of a log file, an API response, or an email header, paste it into your decoder, and get one of these: binascii.Error: Incorrect padding The input is not a valid Base-64 string InvalidCharacterError: The string to be decoded is not correctly encoded or worse, it "works" and gives you hÃ©llo instead of héllo The string is rarely garbage; usually something changed it on the way. This post covers what makes a Base64 string valid, the five problems I run into most, and a small normalizer in Python and JavaScript that fixes the common cases. What "valid Base64" actually means Standard Base64 (RFC 4648 §4) turns every 3 bytes of input into 4 characters from a 64-character alphabet: A-Z a-z 0-9 + / If the input length isn't a multiple of 3, the output is padded with = (one or two of them) so the total length is a multiple of 4. A valid standard string therefore has: Only alphabet characters, plus = at the very end At most two = , and only as trailing padding A length divisible by 4 Here's a quick check in Python: import base64 print ( base64 . b64encode ( b " Hello, World! " )) # b'SGVsbG8sIFdvcmxkIQ==' 13 bytes of input is 4 full groups of 3 plus 1 leftover byte, so you get 20 characters, the last two of which are == . There's also a URL-safe variant (RFC 4648 §5), often called Base64URL, which swaps + for - and / for _ and usually drops the padding. The same bytes encode differently: print ( base64 . b64encode ( b " \xfb\xff\xbf " )) # b'+/+/' print ( base64 . urlsafe_b64encode ( b " \xfb\xff\xbf " )) # b'-_-_' Keep that pair in mind. It comes up again below. A worked example: watching strict decoding fail Python's b64decode has a validate=True flag that makes it strict. Here's what it says about some typical broken inputs: import base64 , binascii for s in [ " SGVsbG8 " , " SGVs bG8= " , " -_-_ " , " SGV=sbG8 " , " SGVsbG8= " ]: try : print ( repr ( s ), base64 . b64decode ( s , validate = True )) except binascii . Error as e : print ( repr ( s ), " ERR " , e ) Output: 'SGVsbG8' ERR Incorrect padding 'SGVs bG8=' ERR Only base64 data is allowed '-_-_' ERR Only base64 data is allowed 'SGV=sbG8' ERR Excess data after padding 'SGVsbG8=' b'Hello' Each failure has a different root cause. The five usual suspects 1. Missing padding. SGVsbG8 is Hello with its = stripped. JWTs, many APIs, and most Base64URL encoders drop padding on purpose. The fix is mechanical: append = until len % 4 == 0 . One catch: a remainder of 1 can never be fixed by padding. A single leftover character carries only 6 bits, which isn't enough for a byte, so the string was truncated. 2. Whitespace and line breaks. MIME (email) wraps Base64 at 76 characters, PEM files wrap at 64, and copy-paste from terminals adds \r\n . Python's default (non-strict) decoder silently drops these characters, while strict decoders reject them. Strip all whitespace before validating. 3. URL-safe characters in a standard decoder. If you see - or _ , it's Base64URL. Translate - → + and _ → / , then fix the padding. 4. A data URI prefix. Strings like data:text/plain;base64,SGVsbG8sIFdvcmxkIQ== include a header that isn't Base64. Drop everything up to and including the first comma. 5. URL encoding on top. If the string went through a query string, = may now be %3D and + may be %2B , or even a space. URL-decode first. A % sign is never valid Base64. And one that isn't a validation error at all: 6. Wrong character set when turning bytes into text. The browser's atob() returns one character per byte (effectively Latin-1), so UTF-8 text with multi-byte characters gets mangled: atob ( " aMOpbGxv " ); // "hÃ©llo" — the bytes are right, the interpretation is wrong The Base64 was fine. The bytes are 68 c3 a9 6c 6c 6f , which is héllo in UTF-8. Decode the bytes with TextDecoder instead. Also remember that valid Base64 doesn't have to be text: it can just as easily be a PNG, a ZIP, or ciphertext. A small normalizer Python: import base64 , re STD = re . compile ( r " [A-Za-z0-9+/]*={0,2} " ) def normalize_b64 ( s : str ) -> bytes : s = s . strip () if s . startswith ( " data: " ): s = s . split ( " , " , 1 )[ 1 ] # drop data URI header s = re . sub ( r " \s+ " , "" , s ) # drop whitespace/newlines s = s . replace ( " - " , " + " ). replace ( " _ " , " / " ) # URL-safe -> standard s = s . rstrip ( " = " ) if len ( s ) % 4 == 1 : raise ValueError ( " impossible length: one leftover character " ) s += " = " * ( - len ( s ) % 4 ) # restore padding if not STD . fullmatch ( s ): raise ValueError ( " illegal characters " ) return base64 . b64decode ( s , validate = True ) print ( normalize_b64 ( " SGVsbG8 " )) # b'Hello' print ( normalize_b64 ( " SGVs \r\n bG8= " )) # b'Hello' print ( normalize_b64 ( " -_-_ " )) # b'\xfb\xff\xbf' print ( normalize_b64 ( " aMOpbGxv " ). decode ( " utf-8 " )) # héllo JavaScript (browser or Node 16+): function decodeBase64Utf8 ( input ) { let s = input . trim (); if ( s . startsWith ( " data: " )) s = s . slice ( s . indexOf ( " , " ) + 1 ); s = s . replace ( / \s +/g , "" ). replace ( /-/g , " + " ). replace ( /_/g , " / " ). replace ( /=+$/ , "" ); if ( s . length % 4 === 1 ) throw new Error ( " Impossible length " ); s += " = " . repeat (( 4 - ( s . length % 4 )) % 4 ); if ( ! /^ [ A-Za-z0-9+ /] *= {0,2} $/ . test ( s )) throw new Error ( " Illegal characters " ); const bytes = Uint8Array . from ( atob ( s ), ( c ) => c . charCodeAt ( 0 )); return new TextDecoder ( " utf-8 " , { fatal : true }). decode ( bytes ); } decodeBase64Utf8 ( " aMOpbGxv " ); // "héllo" decodeBase64Utf8 ( decodeURIComponent ( " SGVsbG8%3D " )); // "Hello" decodeBase64Utf8 ( " data:text/plain;base64,SGVsbG8sIFdvcmxkIQ== " ); // "Hello, World!" With fatal: true , the decoder throws when the bytes aren't valid UTF-8 (for example +/+/ , which decodes to fb ff bf ). That's a useful signal that you're looking at binary data, not a broken string. When to be strict and when to be forgiving Be strict at trust boundaries. If you're accepting Base64 from users or other services, validate with strict rules and reject bad input with a clear error. Forgiving decoders can hide real corruption. Be forgiving when debugging. When you're staring at a string from a log, normalize first, then decode. Don't treat "decodes successfully" as "is Base64". The string test is valid Base64 (it decodes to three bytes, b5 eb 2d ). Lots of ordinary words pass the check. If you need to know whether a field is meant to be Base64, rely on your schema, not a guess. Checking a string quickly When I just want to know what's wrong with a string, I paste it into the Base64 Validator . It checks the character set, padding, length, and whether the string actually decodes, and it handles standard RFC 4648 §4, URL-safe §5, and data URI prefixes. The report shows the detected variant, padding status, character length, decoded byte size, and a text preview. Everything runs client-side in the browser, so nothing you paste is sent to a server. Disclosure: I'm Nagesh and I built base64decodetool.com. If you hit a Base64 failure that isn't covered here, tell me in the comments. I'd like to add it to the checklist.

title: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash Generates and Edits 15-Second Videos in the Gemini API for $0.07 a Second
author: Ishank Choudhary
summary: On November 5, 2026, Google made Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash ( gemini-omni-1.2-flash ) generally available across the Gemini API and Google Cloud. Two weeks after shutting down Veo 3.1 Preview in the developer API on October 22, Google is positioning Omni Flash as its default model for generating, editing and extending video with synchronized audio. Three headline changes stand out: Native 15-second clips , up from 10 seconds in Omni 1.1 Flash, selectable in one-second steps from 3 to 15 seconds. A 30% price cut on video output tokens, dropping 720p generation from about $0.10 per second to roughly $0.07 per second ($12.00 per million video output tokens, down from $17.50). Multi-turn conversational editing and stronger reference adherence , accepting up to 6 reference images and refining clips across turns without starting over. One date in the release notes matters if you already ship on Omni 1.1: on December 3, 2026, every API call to gemini-omni-1.1-flash will automatically route to gemini-omni-1.2-flash . I spent Friday evening wiring gemini-omni-1.2-flash up on Linux with Python 3.12, google-genai 3.0.0, raw REST calls and ffprobe . Because my AI Studio key is on the Free Tier, where Omni 1.2 enforces a hard zero-quota wall, I couldn't render paid clips from my own prompts. Everything else on the wire was testable right now, and the first bug hit in 90 milliseconds. What I tested and where the Free Tier stops My setup and test boundary: Environment: Linux x86_64, Python 3.12.14, google-genai 3.0.0, ffprobe and a Free Tier AI Studio GEMINI_API_KEY . What ran live ($0.00 spend): model discovery ( models.list , models.get ), input token accounting ( countTokens ) across text, reference images, uploaded 720p video and WAV audio, Files API upload latency, pre-quota schema validation on /v1beta/interactions , model-routing checks, stateful chaining and container inspection of Google's raw omni_*.mp4 API samples. What blocked ( HTTP 429 ): all four video generation calls I sent (5s 360p draft, 6s 720p alley tracking shot, 15s 720p timecoded clip via URI delivery, and 6s 2-image reference shot) returned Rate limit exceeded for model gemini-omni-1.2-flash (limit: 0 input tokens per minute on Free Tier) in 0.41 to 0.48 seconds . Omni 1.2 Flash has zero Free Tier quota : 0 RPM and 0 RPD. Even a 3-second 360p draft (~$0.07) requires Paid Tier 1 billing enabled (8 RPM, 40 RPD, doubled from Omni 1.1). If you want to try 15-second clips manually without API billing, Google Vids includes them at no extra cost on Google and Workspace accounts. Because I didn't run on a paid project, I haven't measured live video render times or visual drift on my own prompts. Google also published zero benchmarks comparing 1.2 against 1.1, so treat quality claims as untested until you run your own prompts. Bug #1: Google's Python quickstart 404s out of the box Gemini Omni models run on Google's stateful Interactions API ( /v1beta/interactions ), not generateContent , even though GET /v1beta/models/gemini-omni-1.2-flash (0.17s) still lists ["generateContent", "countTokens"] under supportedGenerationMethods . If you install google-genai 3.0.0 and run the quickstart from Google's Omni docs: from google import genai client = genai . Client () interaction = client . interactions . create ( model = " gemini-omni-1.2-flash " , input = " A marble rolling fast on a chain reaction style track, continuous smooth shot. " , response_format = { " type " : " video " , " duration " : " 5s " , " resolution " : " 360p " }, ) It fails in 0.09 to 0.46 seconds with a 404: NotFoundError: Error code: 404 - {'error': {'message': "Model 'gemini-omni-1.2-flash' not found. Did you mean 'gemini-omni-1.1-flash'?", 'code': 'not_found'}} "Did you mean 'gemini-omni-1.1-flash'?" is a red herring: gemini-omni-1.1-flash 404s on that path too (0.20s). Inspecting client.interactions.sdk_configuration shows why. In google-genai 3.0.0, the Interactions sub-client defaults to Globals(api_version='v1') ( POST /v1/interactions ), where neither Omni 1.1 nor 1.2 exists. Both live only on v1beta . (Importing google.genai on Python 3.12 also emits two SyntaxWarning escape warnings in types.py .) Passing api_version="v1beta" fixes the 404: interaction = client . interactions . create ( api_version = " v1beta " , model = " gemini-omni-1.2-flash " , input = " A marble rolling fast on a chain reaction style track, continuous smooth shot. " , response_format = { " type " : " video " , " duration " : " 5s " , " resolution " : " 360p " , " delivery " : " uri " }, ) Right behind that 404 sits a second SDK catch. When client.interactions.create(api_version="v1beta", ...) hits a 429 , even a permanent limit: 0 Free Tier error, its internal retry loop retries silently for over 90 seconds per call before raising RateLimitError . Two calls hung my script for over three minutes before I killed it. Cap retries in CI so bad keys fail fast. What I measured on the live API Even without paid video output quota, several parts of the gemini-omni-1.2-flash stack respond on a Free Tier key. 1. Real input token counts ( countTokens ) Omni 1.2 Flash bills inputs at $1.50 per million tokens across text, images and video. Calling POST /v1beta/models/gemini-omni-1.2-flash:countTokens returned HTTP 200 in 0.18 to 0.52 seconds : 14-word text prompt: 16 TEXT tokens (0.19s), costing $0.000024 . Two reference PNGs (1280x720 mug card and 800x800 robot sheet) plus 11-token prompt: 527 tokens ( 11 TEXT + 516 IMAGE, or 258 tokens per image , 0.18s), costing $0.00079 . Six reference PNGs (the maximum allowed) plus 16-token prompt: 1,564 tokens ( 16 TEXT + 1,548 IMAGE, 0.20s), costing $0.00235 . Uploaded 5.0-second 720p 24fps MP4 with AAC audio plus edit prompt: Files API upload took 1.13s and reached ACTIVE in 3.49s (2 polls). countTokens returned 1,488 tokens in 0.30s: 13 TEXT + 1,315 VIDEO ( 263 video tokens/s ) + 160 AUDIO ( 32 audio tokens/s ), or 295 media tokens/s . That is $0.00223 for 5s, or about $0.0066 for a 15s input clip. Input tokens are rounding error. Six reference images or a 15-second source video cost under two-thirds of a cent; over 99.5% of your bill is video output. 2. Schema checks that fail fast ( HTTP 400 ) POST /v1beta/interactions validates its request schema before checking quota, returning HTTP 400 in 0.18 to 0.21 seconds : Duration needs "s" : "duration": 5 fails; pass "3s" through "15s" (defaults to "10s" ). Four resolutions: "480p" fails, listing '360p' , '720p' , '1080p' , '4k' . Two aspect ratios: "1:1" fails, listing '16:9' (default) and '9:16' . Five task enums: "video_upscale" fails, listing 'text_to_video' , 'image_to_video' , 'reference_to_video' , 'edit' , 'extend' . Google advises omitting task unless prompting picks the wrong mode, and deprecates <FIRST_FRAME> and <IMAGE_REF_0> control tags. 3. Stateful chaining and silent model routing To test multi-turn state lookup, I created a Turn 1 interaction on /v1beta/interactions with gemini-3-flash-preview ( HTTP 200 in 3.22s , returning v1_Chds... ), then passed that previous_interaction_id into gemini-omni-1.2-flash on Turn 2. A fake ID failed pre-quota with HTTP 400 in 0.32s, while the real v1_... ID passed state lookup across models and hit the Omni 1.2 quota gate in 0.88s. Avoid setting store=false on Turn 1 if you plan to edit later, since disabling storage breaks previous_interaction_id . Sending "model": "gemini-omni-flash-preview" (shut down earlier) returned a 429 naming gemini-omni-1.1-flash (0.52s), confirming the gateway already aliases retired Omni IDs server-side ahead of the December 3 1.1 to 1.2 switch. Output cost math and the 4 MB payload trap Google bills Omni 1.2 Flash video output at $12.00 per million tokens (text and thinking tokens at $9.00 per million): 360p: 1,931 tokens/s, or $0.023/s ($0.12 for 5s, $0.35 for 15s) 720p (default): 5,792 tokens/s, or $0.070/s ($0.42 for 6s, $0.70 for 10s, $1.04 for 15s) 1080p (upsampled): 8,688 tokens/s, or $0.104/s ($0.52 for 5s, $1.56 for 15s) 4K (upsampled): 17,376 tokens/s, or $0.209/s ($1.04 for 5s, $3.13 for 15s) Nine 15-second drafts at 360p ($3.13) cost the same as one 15-second render at 4K ($3.13). Draft at 360p or 720p, refine via previous_interaction_id , and render 1080p or 4K last. Batch API is unsupported. Inspecting four raw omni_*.mp4 samples from Google's API docs ( encoder: Google ) and three launch-blog demos with ffprobe showed why delivery settings matter: Container specs: raw outputs are H.264 ( yuv420p ) at 24 fps with 48 kHz stereo AAC at 2.37 to 4.54 Mbps . The 4 MB inline limit: inline base64 responses cap out at 4 MB . Three of Google's four raw 720p doc samples ( 5.42 MB at 10s, 5.65 MB at 20s, 5.78 MB at 20s) exceed 4 MB; only one 10s clip ( 3.08 MB ) fits. Always pass "delivery": "uri" for 10-to-15-second 720p+ clips and poll GET /v1beta/files/{id} until ACTIVE . Provenance ( SynthID + C2PA ): alongside invisible SynthID watermarking, all four raw API MP4s carry a C2PA JUMBF manifest ( jumdc2pa ) signed by Google Media Processing Services under Google C2PA Root CA G3 . The FFmpeg-reencoded blog demos ( Lavf62.12.102 ) lost their C2PA box, while SynthID survives in the frames. One doc slip: omni_misty_mountains_1080p.mp4 , embedded right under Google's resolution: "1080p" example, is actually 1280x720 in ffprobe . Four doc contradictions and what to fix before December 3 Reading Google's Keyword post, Cloud blog, Gemini API docs and Cloud Agent Platform model card side by side surfaced four mismatches: 15 seconds does not apply to every mode: text, single-image, reference-to-video and edits reach 15 seconds (with 11-to-15s clips limited to 1 3s reference video instead of 3), but first-and-last-frame interpolation stays capped at 3 to 10 seconds . Passing "15s" with two keyframes returns an invalid argument error. Audio references are gated: the DeepMind blog pitches 1-second voice cues, the Cloud blog says audio references need allowlisting , and the Gemini API docs mark audio uploads unsupported —even though countTokens already tokenizes WAV input at 32.5 AUDIO tokens/s. Extended length ( 30s vs 40s ): Gemini API docs cap multi-turn extension at 30 seconds total , while the Cloud model card implies up to 40 seconds . Output token ceiling ( 65,536 vs 260,640 ): models.get lists outputTokenLimit: 65,536 , yet 15s at 720p needs 86,880 tokens and 15s at 4K needs 260,640 , matching the Cloud card's 260,640 limit. Google also notes rough spots on fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics , no support for system instructions, temperature , top_p or negative prompt fields, and EEA/UK/Switzerland blocks on editing uploaded video. If you run gemini-omni-1.1-flash today, four updates get you ahead of the December 3, 2026 automatic reroute: Pass api_version="v1beta" in google-genai 3.0.0 and cap retries so quota errors fail fast. Default to "delivery": "uri" on 10-to-15-second clips at 720p+ to avoid the 4 MB inline cap. Cap UI durations at 3–15s for standard generation and 3–10s for keyframe interpolation and extensions. 4. Strip deprecated <FIRST_FRAME> and <IMAGE_REF_0> tags and test gemini-omni-1.2-flash on staging now, banking the 30% price drop on your own schedule. Originally published on Medium .

title: Windows won't let you own Win+Shift+S. So I hooked the keyboard in Python.
author: Akhouri Anmol Kumar
summary: I wanted one small thing: press Win+Shift+S and get my own screenshot tool instead of Snipping Tool. That turned into a 7,600-line Python project, and a pile of Windows internals that I couldn't find explained in one place. Here are the four that cost me the most hair. 1. RegisterHotKey can't claim Win+Shift+S Every tutorial says to use RegisterHotKey . It works for Ctrl+Alt+D . It silently fails for Win+Shift+S , because the shell reserves that combo. The way around it is a low-level keyboard hook ( WH_KEYBOARD_LL , id 13 ), which sees the key before the shell does: HOOKPROC = ctypes . WINFUNCTYPE ( ctypes . c_ssize_t , ctypes . c_int , ctypes . c_size_t , ctypes . c_ssize_t ) def cb ( nCode , wParam , lParam ): if nCode == 0 and wParam in ( 0x100 , 0x101 , 0x104 , 0x105 ): kb = ctypes . cast ( lParam , ctypes . POINTER ( KBDLLHOOKSTRUCT )). contents if kb . vkCode == 0x53 and win_down () and shift_down (): # S u . keybd_event ( 0xE8 , 0 , 0 , 0 ) # see below u . keybd_event ( 0xE8 , 0 , 2 , 0 ) QTimer . singleShot ( 0 , on_trigger ) # hop back to the Qt thread return 1 # swallow the key return u . CallNextHookEx ( None , nCode , wParam , lParam ) self . _proc = HOOKPROC ( cb ) # keep a reference! hook = u . SetWindowsHookExW ( 13 , self . _proc , k . GetModuleHandleW ( None ), 0 ) Three gotchas worth knowing: Keep a reference to the callback. If HOOKPROC(cb) gets garbage-collected, your app crashes on the next keypress. There's no traceback, it just dies. Swallowing S isn't enough. If you eat the keypress and the user then releases Win , Windows opens the Start menu. The fix is to inject an unassigned virtual key ( 0xE8 ) so Windows thinks Win was used in a combo. Track the key-up too. If you swallow the key-down, you have to swallow its matching key-up, or apps see an orphaned release. I pulled this into a pure function ( snip_hook_decision(...) ) with no ctypes in it, so it's unit-testable. The hook only looks at the specific keys it cares about while Win+Shift are held. Nothing is logged or stored. If you ship a keyboard hook, say that in your README. 2. Keeping your own UI out of your own recording My screen recorder has a floating control bar. Early on, every video started with the recorder recording itself, which looks amateur. Windows 10 (2004+) has a one-line fix: WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE = 0x11 ctypes . windll . user32 . SetWindowDisplayAffinity ( int ( widget . winId ()), WDA_EXCLUDEFROMCAPTURE ) The window stays visible to the user but is invisible to capture APIs. It's best-effort on older builds, so wrap it in try/except and move on. 3. System audio in Python: sounddevice can't do it Recording the microphone is easy. Recording what the PC is playing is not. sounddevice can't do WASAPI loopback. What worked: Source Library Microphone sounddevice System audio (loopback) PyAudioWPatch Mixing + muxing into MP4 imageio-ffmpeg (bundles an ffmpeg binary) The part that matters: don't mix in real time. I record each source to its own WAV on disk, then mix once after the take with ffmpeg's amix . Real-time mixing means two clocks drifting against each other. Post-mixing means a dropped buffer in one stream can't corrupt the other. I also pad or trim each track to exactly the video duration before mixing, because mic and loopback streams never end at the same millisecond. 4. OCR with zero extra installs I wanted "select text from a screenshot" without telling users to install Tesseract. Windows 10/11 already ships an OCR engine: Windows.Media.Ocr . You can reach it from PowerShell, so Python just shells out: subprocess . run ( [ " powershell " , " -NoProfile " , " -ExecutionPolicy " , " Bypass " , " -File " , ps1 ], capture_output = True , timeout = 120 , creationflags = 0x08000000 , # CREATE_NO_WINDOW, no console flash ) The PowerShell script tries the user's language packs first and falls back to whatever recognizer is available. It runs in a QThread , so the UI never freezes. The result: no models to download, no 200 MB dependency, and it works offline. Small things that made it feel finished Recycle Bin, not delete. os.remove is permanent. SHFileOperationW with FOF_ALLOWUNDO sends files to the Recycle Bin, so "delete capture" is never scary. Atomic settings. Write to settings.json.tmp , then os.replace() . A crash mid-write can't corrupt your config. Single instance. A named mutex ( CreateMutexW + check for error 183 ) stops two copies fighting over the same global hotkeys. Autostart is one registry value under HKCU\...\Run . No installer needed. Where all this ended up All of the above lives in ASNIPP , a screenshot tool, screen recorder and editor that sits as a small "Dynamic Island" pill at the top of your screen. The parts I'm proudest of: Screenshots with pen, highlighter, arrows, shapes, text and pixelate (for hiding sensitive info) A color picker with a magnifier loupe, and a pixel ruler Pin-to-screen floating captures Screen recording with system audio and mic, plus live drawing that gets recorded into the video A built-in video editor: trim, speed, reverse, color looks, fades, rotate and GIF export OCR on any capture It's one 7600+ lines of python code packed into .exe, PyQt6, mss for capture and OpenCV for video. If you've ever wondered how far a python desktop app can go, it's a decent case study. 👉 [ https://github.com/Akhouri-Systems/ASNIPP/releases/download/v1.0.0/ASNIPP_v1.zip ] If you've built something with ctypes and Win32, I'd love to hear what bit you. Drop it in the comments.

title: WordPress.com vs WordPress.org: Key Differences, Pros, Cons & Which Is Better?
author: zozothemes
summary: Imagine spending hours choosing a website design, writing your first blog post, and planning your business launch only to discover that your website platform limits the features you need. This is a common problem for beginners who choose a platform before understanding how it works. The choice between WordPress.com vs WordPress.org affects more than where your website is hosted. It determines how much control you have over design, plugins, monetization, performance, maintenance, and future growth. Both options use WordPress, but they offer different ways to build and manage a website. Whether you are starting a personal blog, launching a company website, or creating an online store, this guide explains the differences in practical terms so you can make a confident decision. 1. What Are WordPress.com and WordPress.org? WordPress is a website publishing platform, but its two popular options work differently. WordPress.com is a hosted website service. The hosting environment and much of the technical setup are managed for you. You create an account, choose a plan, select a design, and build your website through its dashboard. The level of customization and access to advanced features depends on the plan you choose. WordPress.org is the home of the open-source WordPress software. You download the software or install it through a web hosting provider, then manage the website using your hosting account and WordPress dashboard. You choose the hosting company, domain, themes, plugins, backups, and many other parts of the setup. For example, a freelance photographer who wants a simple portfolio with minimal technical maintenance may prefer a hosted service. A growing photography studio that needs booking forms, client galleries, SEO tools, and custom integrations may benefit from the flexibility of self-hosted WordPress. The important distinction is that one is a managed hosting service, while the other provides software you can run with a hosting provider. 2. WordPress.com vs WordPress.org: Key Differences at a Glance Before choosing, compare the areas that affect everyday website management. The biggest differences are not about the editor alone; they involve ownership, hosting, customization, costs, and technical responsibility. Feature WordPress.com WordPress.org Hosting Hosting is included You choose a hosting provider Software Cost Plans vary; a free option may be available WordPress software is free Domain Depends on the plan Register a domain separately Maintenance Much of the infrastructure is managed You manage updates and maintenance, or hire help Themes Available options depend on the plan Access to a wide range of free and premium themes Plugins Availability depends on the plan Install compatible plugins as needed Customization Varies by plan and platform limits Extensive control over files and code Backups Features depend on the plan Arrange backups through your host or a plugin Monetization Subject to plan features and platform terms More flexibility, subject to laws and provider terms Technical Control More managed environment Greater control over hosting and configuration A useful way to understand the difference is to think about renting a furnished workspace versus setting up your own office. A managed workspace saves setup time, while your own office gives you more freedom to choose equipment, layout, and services. For many website owners, WordPress.com vs WordPress.org comes down to how much control they need and how much maintenance they are prepared to handle. 3. Hosting, Setup, and Website Management Hosting determines where your website files and database are stored. It also influences performance , security options, backups, and how easily your site can grow. When evaluating WordPress.com vs WordPress.org, hosting is one of the first practical differences to understand. With WordPress.com, hosting is part of the service. You do not need to compare server providers or configure a hosting environment before publishing. This can make the initial setup easier for people who want to focus on writing, publishing, or presenting their business. With WordPress.org, you select a hosting provider and connect your domain to your hosting account. Many providers offer one-click WordPress installation, so the process does not necessarily require advanced technical knowledge. However, you are responsible for choosing a suitable hosting plan and understanding what maintenance your provider handles. Practical example: A local bakery launching its first website may choose managed hosting to get online quickly. If the bakery later needs online ordering, delivery integrations, customer accounts, and advanced analytics, a self-hosted setup may provide more room to configure those tools. Before selecting a hosting plan, check: Storage and bandwidth limits. Server performance and available caching. SSL certificate support. Backup frequency and restoration options. Support availability and migration assistance. Renewal costs, not just introductory pricing. The right hosting arrangement should match your expected traffic and website requirements—not simply the lowest advertised price. 4. Themes, Plugins, and Customization Options Your theme controls the visual structure of your website, while plugins add functionality such as contact forms, booking systems, SEO tools, security features, and online shopping. On WordPress.com, the themes and plugin capabilities available to you depend on the plan and its current feature restrictions. Check the plan details before purchasing, especially if your project relies on a particular plugin, custom code, or third-party integration. With WordPress.org, you can choose from the WordPress theme and plugin ecosystem and install compatible products through your dashboard. You can also work with a developer to customize templates, add functionality, or build features for a specific business workflow. For example, imagine a travel agency that wants destination pages, enquiry forms, tour listings, customer reviews, and a booking process. A suitable theme can provide the starting layout, while selected plugins can add the required features. The agency should still check compatibility, support, update history, and performance before installing each tool. A flexible setup is useful, but installing too many plugins can create maintenance and compatibility problems. Choose tools based on genuine requirements rather than adding features simply because they are available. If design flexibility and access to a broad range of website tools are important, WordPress.com vs WordPress.org is a comparison worth making before committing to a platform. 5. Pricing, Ownership, and Monetization The cost of a website is more than its starting subscription or hosting fee. Consider the total cost over a year, including the domain, hosting, premium themes , plugins, email services, backups, and professional support. WordPress.com offers different plans with features and prices that can change. A free option may be suitable for experimenting, while a paid plan may be necessary for a custom domain or specific business features. Review the current plan limits and renewal terms before making a decision. WordPress.org software itself is free, but running a self-hosted website involves other expenses. You may pay for hosting, a domain, premium design products, paid extensions, and maintenance services. You can begin with a modest setup and add paid tools as your needs develop. Potential Expense Hosted Service Self-Hosted Website WordPress Software Included in the service Free Hosting Included in the plan Purchased separately Domain Depends on the plan Usually purchased separately Premium Design Depends on available options Optional Plugins and Extensions Depends on plan access Free and paid options Maintenance More infrastructure is managed Owner or service provider manages it When comparing WordPress.com vs WordPress.org, also understand the difference between platform access and website ownership. With a self-hosted installation, you have direct access to your website files and database through your hosting provider. You still need to maintain backups and keep copies of important data. For monetization, consider the business model you want to use. This could include selling products, displaying advertising, publishing paid content, accepting bookings, or collecting leads. Each platform has its own features, policies, and limitations, so verify that your intended revenue model is supported before building around it. 6. SEO, Performance, Security, and Maintenance When assessing WordPress.com vs WordPress.org, remember that a website platform does not automatically guarantee high Google rankings . Search visibility depends on useful content, search intent, technical quality, website experience, and consistent maintenance. Both options can support SEO activities, but the tools and level of technical control available may differ. Your website should have clear page titles, descriptive URLs, helpful internal links, accessible content, optimized images, and a logical heading structure. For example, a WordPress blog publishing tutorials should organize articles into relevant categories, link related guides together, compress images, and make pages easy to navigate on mobile devices. These improvements help readers find information and help search engines understand the website. Performance also matters. A slow website can frustrate visitors, especially on mobile connections. Use a reliable hosting environment, a lightweight theme, optimized images, suitable caching, and only the plugins you need. Security requires ongoing attention, particularly when you manage your own hosting environment. Follow these practices: Use strong, unique administrator passwords and enable two-factor authentication where available. Keep WordPress core, themes, and plugins updated. Remove inactive themes and plugins you no longer need. Maintain regular backups and test restoration. Use SSL and reputable security tools. Restrict administrator access to people who need it. A managed service can reduce some infrastructure responsibilities, but it does not remove the need for secure passwords, careful account access, and safe publishing practices. A self-hosted website gives you more control, but that control comes with more responsibility. 7. Pros and Cons: Which Option Fits Your Needs? There is no single solution for every website. The better choice depends on your budget, technical confidence, growth plans, and the features you expect to use. WordPress.com advantages Hosting and much of the infrastructure are managed for you. Initial setup is convenient for beginners. You can focus on publishing without configuring a separate hosting account. Different plans provide options as your requirements change. WordPress.com limitations Advanced features may require a higher-tier plan. Plugin and customization access depends on current plan restrictions. You have less control over the hosting environment. Costs can increase as you need more features. WordPress.org advantages The software is free and open source. You choose your hosting provider and domain registrar. A broad theme and plugin ecosystem supports different website types. You have greater control over customization, files, and integrations. You can select services that fit your budget and technical needs. WordPress.org limitations Hosting and domain costs are your responsibility. You need a plan for updates, backups, and security. Poor hosting or excessive plugins can affect performance. Some customizations may require technical knowledge or developer support. For a personal blog with straightforward needs, a managed service may be enough. For a business website , membership site, online store, directory, or project that depends on custom functionality, self-hosted WordPress is often a stronger long-term fit. 8. Which Is the Best WordPress Platform for Your Website? The Best WordPress platform is the one that supports your actual goals without adding unnecessary cost or complexity. To identify the Best WordPress platform for your project, start by listing the features you need now and the ones you are likely to need in the next year. Choose WordPress.com if: You want a straightforward setup with hosting included. You prefer having much of the infrastructure managed. Your website needs are relatively simple. The plan you select includes the features you require. Choose WordPress.org if: You want greater control over themes, plugins, and customization. You plan to build a business website or online store with specific workflows. You need access to website files and database through your hosting provider. You are comfortable managing maintenance or paying someone to do it. A real-world decision: A student creating a personal writing portfolio may value simplicity over advanced configuration. A digital agency building websites for clients may need custom layouts, staging environments, specialized plugins, and hosting choices. Their requirements are different, so their platform decisions can be different too. If you are still unsure which is the Best WordPress platform for your situation, write down your must-have features—such as a custom domain, booking functionality, ecommerce, email marketing , or custom integrations—and check whether the platform and plan support each one. This simple step can prevent an expensive migration later. Frequently Asked Questions 1. Is WordPress.com the same as WordPress.org? No. WordPress.com is a hosted website service, while WordPress.org provides open-source software that you can install with a hosting provider. Both use WordPress, but hosting, customization, and maintenance responsibilities differ. 2. Is WordPress.org free to use? Yes. The WordPress software is free and open source. However, a self-hosted website generally requires a domain and hosting, and you may choose to pay for premium themes, plugins, or professional support. 3. Can I use plugins on WordPress.com? Plugin availability depends on the current WordPress.com plan and its feature rules. Check the plan comparison and confirm that the specific plugin you need is supported before subscribing. 4. Which option is better for business websites? A self-hosted website can be a strong choice for businesses that need extensive customization, integrations, ecommerce features, or control over hosting. A hosted plan may suit a business with simpler requirements and a preference for managed infrastructure. 5. Can I move my website from WordPress.com to WordPress.org? Yes. A website can be migrated, but the process may involve exporting content, setting up hosting, importing pages and posts, transferring media, configuring the domain, and checking redirects. Some design elements, plugins, and features may need to be recreated. Always make a backup and test the new site before changing DNS settings. Conclusion Choosing between these platforms is ultimately about balancing convenience with control. A managed service can make it easier to get started, while a self-hosted website gives you more freedom to choose your hosting, design tools, and functionality as your project grows. Before deciding, consider your budget, technical comfort, required features, and long-term plans. Compare the current plan limits and hosting costs rather than choosing based on the name alone. Find a design that matches your project, customize it around your brand, and create a website that is ready to grow with your business. Ready to Build Your WordPress Website? title: A broken-link and SEO audit of your whole site, with a ranked fix list for your developer
author: Aurelix Solutions
summary: Most sites collect small SEO problems quietly: a page that now 404s, a link to a partner site that died, a title that grew past 60 characters, a noindex left on after a migration, a new section nobody added to the sitemap. None of them is urgent on its own, which is why they pile up. What a site owner or an agency needs is not a 40-page report but a short list, worst first, with the exact URLs to fix. This post sets that up as a scheduled audit in Python, then compares the SEO audit and broken-link tools on the Apify Store using the prices their Store pages listed at the time of writing. Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built the Broken Link Crawler & SEO Audit . It's a paid tool (prices below). Check each Store page before you buy: prices change. What one run returns You give it one site. It reads the site's XML sitemaps (from robots.txt or /sitemap.xml ), follows internal links on the same host up to maxPages , and returns: One page row per URL : status_code , redirects , title and title_length , meta_description and its length, h1_count , canonical_url , noindex , word_count , link and image counts, broken_links (each with its URL and status code), images_missing_alt_count , in_sitemap , response_time_ms , and issues : the issue codes on that page, most severe first. One summary row : pages_audited , health_score (the share of pages with no high or medium issue), status-code counts, and issues ranked by severity and pages affected, each with up to five example URLs. Broken means a real 404/410, a 5xx or a dead host. Links that answer 401, 403 or 429 (common for sites that block automated checks) are counted as unverified, so they don't clutter the fix list. To track progress, save the input as a task in the Apify Console and schedule it weekly or monthly, then compare the summary rows: health_score and the pages count of each issue. There is no built-in diff between runs. title: Why Your Hotel's Channel Manager Is the Most Important Line of Code You'll Ship This Year
author: ZANISS SOFTWARES
summary: If you've ever built an integration that has to be right 100% of the time or someone loses money, you already understand why hotel channel managers are an underrated engineering problem. Here's the shape of it: a hotel has, say, 40 rooms. Those 40 rooms are listed on MakeMyTrip, Booking.com, Goibibo, and the hotel's own website. The moment a guest books room 12 on any one of those four surfaces, the other three need to know room 12 is gone — ideally within seconds, never with a multi-minute lag, and never with a silent failure that lets two guests show up for the same room on the same night (the industry calls this an "overbooking," and it is exactly as bad as it sounds for a 40-room property with no overflow capacity). The naive approach is a cron job that polls each OTA's inventory API every few minutes and reconciles. It mostly works until volume spikes during a festival weekend, at which point race conditions between two near-simultaneous bookings on two different channels become a real, recurring bug — not a theoretical one. The approach that actually holds up in production treats the property's own inventory table as the single source of truth and pushes availability deltas outward on every state change, with OTA webhooks (where available) supplementing rather than replacing that push. Idempotency keys on every write matter more here than in almost any other CRUD system I've worked on, because a retried webhook that double-decrements inventory is a financial incident, not a log line. On a recent build for a multi-property hotel group in India, we scoped this channel manager layer at roughly ₹9–22 lakh depending on how many OTAs and properties were in play — meaningfully cheaper than licensing an enterprise PMS like Opera for a mid-sized group, while giving the client full ownership of the sync logic instead of being locked into a vendor's black box. Treat that range as a starting point rather than a quote: the number of OTAs, each OTA's certification process and your property count move it more than anything else. The other half of the stack — GST-compliant billing, a guest CRM, and WhatsApp-based guest messaging — all hang off that same inventory core, which is the real argument for building this as one coherent system rather than bolting together five SaaS tools that each have their own idea of "the truth." We wrote up the full cost breakdown and build timeline here: https://zanisssoftwares.com/blog/travel-hospitality-software-development-india-2026 Curious what other engineers here have run into with inventory-sync systems that have real financial consequences on a race condition — booking platforms, ticketing, limited-inventory e-commerce. The patterns rhyme a lot more than I expected going in.

title: I ran two OCR engines and a BERT model entirely in the browser — here's what I learned
author: karthik valluri
summary: Every day, someone pastes a dashboard screenshot into Slack, a Jira ticket, or a slide deck with customer names, emails, and revenue figures still perfectly readable. The usual fix is a redaction tool — and almost every redaction tool uploads your screenshot to a server, which is exactly the thing you were trying to avoid. So I built VaultSnip : a free, open-source tool that finds and blurs sensitive text in screenshots. The constraint I set myself: everything runs on your device. No backend, no account, no upload. The whole app is static files on Cloudflare Pages; your screenshot never leaves the browser tab. That constraint forced me to run a full ML pipeline client-side. Here's what that actually took. The pipeline: two OCR engines and a PII model, all in the tab To decide what to blur, you first need to know what text is in the image and where. VaultSnip layers three engines, each running in a Web Worker: Tesseract.js does the fast first pass. Masks land in a few seconds, so the user sees results immediately. PP-OCRv5 (PaddleOCR's mobile detection + recognition models, as ONNX) catches what Tesseract misses — small print, low-contrast labels, text inside chart chrome. I run the official ONNX exports through ONNX Runtime Web and wrote the DB post-processing and CTC decoding myself in TypeScript. A BERT-small PII model (int8-quantized ONNX, via Transformers.js) classifies the recognized text: is this a person's name, an email, an ID, a company? That decides what gets masked versus left alone. A design rule that mattered more than any model choice: later passes only ever add masks, never remove them. The user watches the screenshot get progressively safer, and an engine disagreement can't un-redact something. Lesson 1: cross-origin isolation is the real price of admission ONNX Runtime Web's threaded SIMD build needs SharedArrayBuffer , and browsers only give you that when the page is cross-origin isolated — Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp headers on everything. That sounds like two lines of config. In practice it means every resource you load — every script, every wasm file, every model weight — must either be same-origin or explicitly opt in. It shaped the entire architecture: all models are bundled and served from the same origin, nothing is pulled from a CDN at runtime. Which turned out to be a feature. "No requests to third-party servers" stopped being a promise and became something you can verify in the Network tab. Lesson 2: model size is a UX problem, not a bandwidth problem The int8-quantized BERT is small by ML standards, and the PP-OCRv5 mobile models are a few megabytes each, gzipped. Users will wait for that once — if the app is honest about it and useful before the download finishes. That's why the layering matters: Tesseract.js (which is comparatively tiny) delivers first masks in seconds while the heavier models are still warming up. The slow part runs while the user is already getting value. Lesson 3: measure what you miss, and publish it Any detection pipeline misses things. Most tools in this space deal with that by never mentioning it. I went the other way: the repo has an automated benchmark that renders fictional dashboards, runs the full pipeline, and measures exactly how much readable text area survives unmasked. Right now that's about 0.25% of readable area , and the number is published in the repo's ACCURACY.md, failure cases included. This felt risky ("my tool's README admits it's imperfect!") and has been nothing but positive. Users trust a published 0.25% far more than an implied 0%, and the benchmark doubles as a regression gate in CI — no change ships if the number gets worse. Lesson 4: the replica — editing pixels in place Blurring is fine for chat, but sometimes you need a screenshot that still looks real — for a demo, a tutorial, a portfolio. VaultSnip's "replica" mode replaces each sensitive value, in place, with a synthetic one: same position, same font size, same color and alignment, with plausible fake data (via Faker, also running locally). The hard rule, enforced by a pixel-diff e2e test: zero changed pixels outside the replaced text boxes. No redrawing charts, no reconstructed layouts. A bar-chart edge that runs through a text box survives the replacement. The replica is the original image, surgically edited — which is the only way it stays believable. What it became What started as a web page is now also a Chrome/Edge extension (same pipeline, plus one-key blurring of charts on live pages) and a Windows desktop app (Tauri 2, with a global hotkey that snips any screen region straight into the masker). All of it Apache-2.0, all of it offline-capable. Try it (no sign-up): https://vaultsnip.pages.dev Source: https://github.com/karthikvalluri85/vaultsnip karthikvalluri85 / vaultsnip Turn sensitive report snips into client-safe replicas VaultSnip Blur sensitive text in any screenshot. Free, offline, in your browser. Paste a screenshot of a dashboard, report, table or app. VaultSnip finds names, numbers, emails and IDs and masks them on your device , shows the first masks within seconds, keeps checking in the background, and gives you a masked image you can copy straight into Slack, Teams, a ticket or a slide. Nothing is uploaded and nothing is stored. Try it: https://vaultsnip.pages.dev (no sign-up, no key, no upload) · Chrome · Edge · Hugging Face Works with screenshots of Power BI, Tableau, Looker, Qlik, Excel, Google Sheets, Salesforce, Jira, PDF report pages and any other app on your screen. On the desktop: a small app with a hotkey. Press Ctrl+Alt+V (Control+Option+V on a Mac), drag over the part of the screen you want, and once the check passes the masked image is on your clipboard.
